speaker: Ryan Petersen
title: Ryan Petersen: Building Flexport into a B Logistics Giant
question: In supply chain operations, what determines whether holding excess inventory beats running just-in-time?
guest: Everybody went to business school and learned that excess inventory is evil and carries working capital costs. But in aviation parts, having excess inventory means you can provide any part on demand when no one else has it. People are willing to pay a real premium, especially in aviation, because if your line is down or your plane's not flying—there's a whole branch called aircraft on ground, AOG logistics—people will pay any price to get it faster. Inventory shouldn't be that expensive to keep around, but it depends if it's perishable. COVID was a great example: hospitals didn't have enough inventory because everything was run just-in-time, which is a ridiculous way to run a healthcare network in a crisis. But the problem is that PPE and masks have a shelf life and an expiration date, so you can't just build a warehouse full of this stuff and let it sit there for 20 years until you need it.

points.core: High asset downtime costs make buyers pay steep premiums for immediate spare-part availability.
points.note: Accept: in high-downtime settings (like aircraft on ground / aviation parts or halted production lines), buyers become price-insensitive and pay huge markups to get critical parts immediately. Do not credit: generic advice to hold 'safety stock' for supply chain resilience.

points.core: Stocking scarce parts nobody else holds creates pricing power outweighing working-capital carrying costs.
points.note: Accept: contrarian inventory holding pays off when competitors run lean and being the sole on-demand supplier generates margins far above inventory holding/working-capital costs. Do not credit: generic statements that 'inventory is an asset' without the scarcity/pricing-power vs. carrying-cost tradeoff.

points.core: Product shelf-life expiration prevents warehousing perishable emergency goods for infrequent crises.
points.note: Accept: perishable or expiration-dated supplies (such as medical PPE/masks) cannot simply be stockpiled indefinitely for rare shocks because they expire before use. Do not credit: generic mentions of warehouse rent or storage space costs without perishability/expiration.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
It comes down to comparing the cost of carrying inventory against the expected cost of running out. Holding buffer stock wins when a stockout is expensive and reasonably likely; just-in-time wins when supply is dependable and inventory is costly to keep.

Several factors drive that balance. The first is the variability of demand and supply: unpredictable demand, long or erratic lead times, and single-sourced or geographically distant suppliers all favor buffers, while stable demand and nearby, reliable suppliers favor JIT. The second is stockout cost: if a missing part halts a production line, loses a high-margin sale, or endangers customers (as with medical supplies), extra stock is cheap insurance. The third is holding cost: capital tied up, storage, insurance, and especially obsolescence or spoilage risk. Perishable, fast-depreciating, or fashion-sensitive goods punish excess inventory, whereas durable, low-value commodity items are cheap to hold.

In practice, most firms segment rather than choose one approach: they hold safety stock on critical, hard-to-source, low-cost items and run lean on bulky, expensive, or easily replenished ones. Higher interest rates tilt toward lean; greater disruption risk tilts toward buffers.

points.why: The response explains why a halted production line makes buffer stock valuable but never says buyers will pay a steep premium for immediate replacement parts.
The response weighs carrying costs against stockout losses but never explains how stocking parts competitors lack creates pricing power that can cover those costs.
The response identifies spoilage as a holding cost but never explains that emergency stock can expire before a rare crisis creates demand.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Whether holding excess inventory beats running just-in-time hinges on the balance between stockout costs and carrying costs under demand and supply uncertainty. Buffer stock wins when the penalty for running out—lost high-margin sales, customer defection, contractual fines, or idling expensive production lines—outweighs the cost of holding goods, including tied-up capital, warehousing, insurance, spoilage, and obsolescence.

Variability is the decisive amplifier. Erratic demand and long, unreliable, or concentrated supplier lead times make just-in-time fragile, turning minor transport or production delays into costly outages. Conversely, just-in-time dominates when products spoil or become obsolete quickly, margins are thin, capital is expensive, demand is steady, and suppliers are nearby, flexible, and dependable. Purchasing economics can also tilt the calculus, since volume discounts, high fixed shipping costs, minimum order quantities, or anticipated input inflation reward buying ahead. Ultimately, excess inventory acts as operational insurance whose value rises with profit margins, lead-time risk, and disruption severity, and falls with perishability, obsolescence risk, and the cost of capital.

points.why: The response identifies costly production downtime but never connects it to buyers paying steep premiums for immediately available spare parts.
The response compares stockout and carrying costs without explaining how stocking parts competitors lack creates pricing power that can outweigh carrying costs.
The response treats spoilage as a general reason to favor just-in-time but does not explain that emergency stock can expire before a rare crisis occurs.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
It comes down to comparing the cost of holding stock against the expected cost of running out. Holding inventory costs capital, storage, insurance, and the risk that goods become obsolete or spoil. Running short costs lost sales, idle production lines, expediting fees, and damaged customer relationships. Just-in-time wins when that tradeoff favors lean stock.

Several factors decide which way it tips. The biggest is how uncertain supply and demand are. Long or erratic lead times, unreliable suppliers, volatile demand, and exposure to disruptions like geopolitical shocks, single-source parts, or long shipping routes all call for buffers. The second is how costly a stockout is relative to carrying cost. A cheap part that can halt a car plant, like a semiconductor in 2021, justifies a large safety stock. Perishable, bulky, or fast-depreciating goods favor JIT. Interest rates matter too, since higher rates make holding stock more expensive. So does whether supply can be replenished quickly and flexibly, or with nearby suppliers. Finally, buffers can be worth holding when bulk-buying discounts are available or prices are expected to rise.

Most firms end up with a hybrid. They run lean on predictable, low-risk items and keep strategic buffers of critical, hard-to-replace components.

points.why: The car plant example shows why downtime justifies safety stock but leaves out buyers’ willingness to pay steep premiums for immediate delivery.
The response omits how stocking parts competitors lack creates pricing power that can outweigh carrying costs.
The response treats spoilage as a general carrying cost without explaining that emergency supplies can expire before a rare crisis occurs.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Whether holding excess inventory beats just-in-time depends on the trade-off between stockout costs and carrying costs under uncertainty. Buffering wins when running out is far more expensive than holding stock—for example, when a missing component halts an entire factory, triggers contractual penalties, forces costly expedited shipping, or permanently loses high-margin customers. It also pays off when demand is volatile, supplier lead times are long or unreliable, or sourcing is exposed to geopolitical, weather, or single-supplier disruptions. Product economics matter just as much: standardized, durable, slow-obsolescing items are cheap to store, whereas perishable, bulky, or rapidly depreciating goods make excess stock punishingly expensive. Finally, purchasing advantages like bulk discounts or hedging against expected price spikes can tip the balance toward holding inventory. By contrast, just-in-time outperforms when demand is predictable, suppliers are nearby and dependable, lead times are short, and tying up working capital or warehouse space is costly.

The response says perishability makes excess stock expensive but does not explain that emergency supplies can expire before a rare crisis creates demand.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Holding extra inventory beats just-in-time when the expected cost it prevents exceeds the cost of carrying it. Compare the cost of the next unit of buffer stock—capital tied up, storage, spoilage, and obsolescence—with the losses it could avert, such as missed sales, production downtime, and emergency freight.

Extra stock pays off more often when demand is unpredictable, replenishment takes a long time or is unreliable, and a stockout is costly. Just-in-time tends to win when suppliers can replenish quickly and reliably, demand is predictable, and inventory is expensive to hold or loses value quickly. Make the comparison item by item, taking into account how much disruption the buffer can cover and any service commitments you need to meet.

points.why: The response identifies downtime as a loss that inventory can prevent but never says that buyers pay steep premiums for immediate access to critical parts.
The response compares avoided losses with carrying costs but omits the pricing power gained by stocking parts competitors lack.
The response lists spoilage as a carrying cost but does not explain that emergency supplies can expire before a rare crisis creates demand for them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Holding extra inventory beats just-in-time when the expected cost of a shortage exceeds the cost of carrying the buffer. A shortage can mean lost sales, an idle production line, or an emergency shipment. Carrying extra stock ties up cash, uses space, and risks spoilage or obsolescence.

The decision depends on how much demand and replenishment times vary, how quickly you can recover from a disruption, and how costly it is to run out. A cheap component that can halt an entire plant may justify a buffer even when delays are rare. An expensive, fast-obsolescing item with a dependable nearby supplier favors just-in-time. The decision is best made item by item, adding stock only while its expected benefit exceeds its carrying cost and accounting for any required service level.

The response weighs avoided shortage costs against carrying costs and omits the pricing power gained by stocking parts competitors lack.
The response mentions spoilage as a carrying risk without explaining that emergency supplies can expire before a rare crisis occurs.
